title: Quantum twisting microscopy as a momentum-resolved probe of quantum geometry and sublattice symmetries
authors: Lucas V. Pupim, Mathias S. Scheurer
abstract: In two-dimensional (2D) flat-band systems, as engineered, for instance, by stacking and twisting van der Waals materials, the momentum dependence of the Bloch states is a key factor in determining the interaction-induced emergence of different phases. Hence, methods of probing this form of ''quantum geometry'' are crucial to understanding these systems. Yet, extracting the momentum dependence of the underlying quantum geometric tensor from measurements is challenging in 2D. Here, we propose employing a quantum twisting microscope (QTM) with a sublattice-polarized tip to fill this gap. We show how expectation values of sublattice Pauli matrices can be probed across the scanned momentum path. This allows for the direct measurement of crucial symmetries characterizing the different candidate instabilities in graphene-based moiré systems. We furthermore show that the quantum metric component along the scan direction can also be extracted; the full quantum geometric tensor is also accessible, given that more than one sublattice polarization can be used. Our work illustrates the potential and extends the versatility of the QTM approach. If implemented in future experiments, this would provide unprecedented access to the symmetry signatures of the correlated phases and to the underlying quantum geometry in twisted bilayer graphene and related systems.
summary: This work introduces the Quantum Twisting Microscope (QTM) as a novel tool to probe the quantum geometry and sublattice symmetries in 2D flat-band materials like twisted bilayer graphene. By using a sublattice-polarized tip, the technique allows for the direct measurement of Pauli matrix expectation values. This capability enables researchers to reconstruct the full quantum geometric tensor, providing deep insights into correlated electronic phases.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a technique to measure the momentum dependence of the quantum geometric tensor and sublattice symmetries in 2D flat-band systems.
main_result: The authors propose and demonstrate that a Quantum Twisting Microscope (QTM) with a sublattice-polarized tip can directly measure sublattice Pauli matrix expectation values, allowing for the reconstruction of the full quantum geometric tensor.
method: The method relies on calculating the tunneling current ($I$) using Fermi's golden rule, which is then analyzed by measuring linear combinations of tunneling terms derived from the sublattice-polarized tip Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The study focuses on 2D flat-band systems, particularly graphene-based moiré superlattices like twisted bilayer graphene (TBG). The physics is modeled using Bloch states ($\xi_S(\mathbf{k})$) and analyzed via tunneling between the sample and the tip.
key_observables: Sublattice Pauli matrix expectation values ($\langle \sigma_i angle$), components of the quantum geometric tensor ($Q_{ij}(k)$), and the layer weight ($p_S(k)$).
important_parameters: Twist angle ($	heta$), bias voltage ($eV$), and the gap induced by the tip polarization ($\Delta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the sample and tip have graphene-like symmetries, and approximations are made regarding the integration of momentum sums into integrals.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the QTM setup, the energetic conditions for momentum resolution, and show the near-constant weight of the top layer component ($p_S(k)$) along the scanned path for TBG.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the measurement challenge in 2D flat-band systems to detailing the QTM setup, deriving the current measurement formula, and finally showing how linear combinations of measurements allow for the extraction of sublattice symmetries and the full quantum metric tensor.
why_interesting: The technique provides unprecedented, symmetry-sensitive access to the underlying quantum geometry of correlated phases in moiré materials, which is crucial for understanding correlated electron physics.
